en: Now begins the *Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpa*. Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa! Having prostrated before Prakṛti and the pure Puruṣa, this work is composed.
This lamp of the principles of Sāṃkhya has been composed by me for the benefit of others.

Indeed, in this world, those who are weary from the exertion of studying the Sāṃkhya treatises— like those whose means of crossing have been destroyed by the current— and who are deprived of the boat of knowledge regarding its system, sink in the ocean of words without any other support; therefore, I shall reveal this [work], which contains many meanings in few syllables and serves as the means for crossing over that ocean while illuminating the entire system of Sāṃkhya.

For those who are indolent in the study of the *Kāpila-tantra* yet desire to understand its system, this very treatise should be thoroughly examined; for everything [required] is to be understood right here, even without the effort that yields results from extremely fierce merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), since no effort is observed toward an object already obtained without exertion.
And it has been said by the Sāṃkhya teachers:
If one should find honey right here on the palm of one's hand, why would one go to the mountain?
When the desired object is already accomplished, what wise person would exert effort?
Some say that since it is improper to accomplish an object that can be achieved by a direct path through a circuitous one;
however, those whose minds are distressed by the impact of the threefold suffering first desire merely the means for its cessation,
which we shall demonstrate hereafter.
And there are three kinds of suffering: internal, external, and celestial.

Among these, the internal is twofold: bodily and mental. The bodily arises from the imbalance of wind, bile, and phlegm; the mental has its causes in desire, anger, greed, delusion, envy, despondency, and the failure to perceive the excellence of objects.
Because it is to be accomplished by internal means, suffering is designated as "internal" (*ādhyātmika*).
Suffering to be accomplished by divine means (*brāhma*) is also twofold:
that which pertains to living beings (*ādhibhautika*) and that which pertains to the celestial or atmospheric realm (*ādhidaivika*).
Among these, the physical (*ādhibhautika*) is caused by humans, birds, reptiles, and stationary beings;
the supernatural (*ādhidaivika*) is caused by possession by spirits such as *piśācas*, *rākṣasas*, *vināyakas*, and *grahas*.
All of this is mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
This suffering is a specific transformation of *rajas*; because it is subject to constant transformation, it cannot be said that this [suffering] is eternal and thus incapable of being suppressed.

Nevertheless, its suppression can indeed be achieved through a means, and that means is nothing other than the knowledge of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* produced by the *śāstra*. Therefore, that *śāstra*...
And the meaning of the title is fourfold, as follows:
Or perhaps some object is not even the fundamental nature itself.
But for some, there is a transformation, as in the case of the root [of a plant].
That [intellect] is the root and the primary cause of everything, but not that [Self].
There might be some other cause for this, according to valid cognition.
Whether it be established in suchness or not, it does not cause harm to the root.
If [the effect] were to exist as its own cause,
then because it would be the cause in relation to itself, it would have to be both prior (due to being the cause) and posterior (due to being the effect); thus, this is impossible.
If it were possessed of a cause, there would be a contradiction with the Vedic scripture which aims to establish its unborn nature, stating: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black.
Furthermore, that which produces is *prakṛti*, namely *pradhāna*, the state of equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

A certain entity is both *prakṛti* (cause) and *vikṛti* (effect); this refers to the group consisting of seven members—the *mahat-tattva*, *ahaṅkāra*, and the five *tanmātras*—which is the *prakṛti* of some and the *vikṛti* of others.

For example, the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) is both the material cause and the transformation of the ego (ahaṅkāra), while being a modification of the Root Nature (mūla-prakṛti). Likewise, the ego is the material cause and the transformation of the five subtle elements (tanmātras) and the sense organs, while being a modification of the Great Principle. Similarly, the five subtle elements are the material causes of the gross elements, such as space and the rest, and are transformations of the ego. The group consisting of the five gross elements and the eleven sense organs—numbering sixteen—is a mere transformation and is not the material cause of anything.

[Objection: But surely, transformations such as cows, jars, and trees are perceived even in the case of earth and the other elements; likewise, specific transformations such as curd and sprouts are perceived in milk, seeds, and so forth. How then can it be said that these [earth, etc. possess only the status of being "transformations" (vikṛti)? [Reply: No, for here "being a material cause" (prakṛtitva) is accepted as the state of being the material substrate for a different principle (tattvāntara). This, however, does not apply to these [earth, etc.], because cows, jars, and the like are gross and perceptible by the senses.
Because they are identical [in nature], there is no difference in principle between them and earth and the other elements.
And it is stated in the *Tattvakaumudī*: "Since all things such as cows and jars share the same qualities of grossness and perceptibility by the senses, they do not constitute a separate principle.

However, the *puruṣa* is not the *prakṛti* (primordial cause) of anything because it is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*), nor is it a modification (*vikṛti*) because it is eternal; otherwise, its manifestation would depend on means for accomplishment, like a jar.
For it is accepted that an object devoid of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is like a man’s horn;

therefore, the Sāṅkhya teachers have accepted three kinds of means of valid cognition as the proof for the aforementioned objects of knowledge: namely, perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), and authoritative testimony (āptavacana).
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) accepted by other disputants are included within these very three.
And it has been said: "Because all means of valid cognition are established";
the meaning is that because all the means of valid cognition admitted by other disputants are established as being included within these three alone.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the pervasion—that whatever perception does not operate upon is absolutely non-existent—is well-established in instances such as the horns of a hare or the hair of a tortoise? Since the Pradhāna is likewise unestablished by perception, its absolute non-existence is logical, just like that of a sky-flower and the like. [Reply: No, for there is no apprehension of a pervasion such that "whatever is beyond the range of perception is absolutely non-existent."

Otherwise, it would follow that for one who has departed from the home and, no longer seeing his house, wealth, sons, cattle, wife, and so forth—which serve as the means of happiness—his heart is consumed by the sorrow of the certainty regarding their destruction, he would die weeping; yet such is not the case.
Furthermore, is "being an object of perception" a reason for existence in the sense of being an object of all perceptions, or in the sense of being an object of some perception?
Not the first [alternative], for it is not possible for any non-yogi to apprehend through direct perception an object situated in another house, another place, or another time;

otherwise, everyone would be omniscient. Since the mind of another is not directly perceptible, it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to determine whether everything is grasped by everyone through direct perception or not, and thus doubt would never cease.

Nor is the last [alternative] tenable, because it is fallacious; for it is not possible that simply because a gavaya was not perceived by someone staying in a city, there could be a denial of that same animal when it is actually perceived by a forest-dweller.
And as it has been said by the author of the *Līlāvatī*: "Because of doubt regarding the non-perception by all, and because of the fallacy of one's own non-perception.
Therefore, that which is absolutely non-existent is that wherein perception—qualified by the absence of anything contrary to its operation—does not occur.

It is possible to determine [the cause], but not merely from the non-occurrence of perception; otherwise, there would be the absolute non-existence of supersensible things such as the Puruṣa, Pradhāna, Mahat, heaven, apūrva, and the deities.
Thus, in the case of perceiving a bird flying in the sky, excessive distance alone is the obstacle; likewise, in the case of perceiving collyrium on the eye, excessive proximity is the obstacle;
similarly, in the perception of color, sound, and so forth, blindness, deafness, and the like are obstacles; and likewise, in the perception of objects, [the absence of] the mind [is an obstacle].

The pervasion by desire and so forth is as follows: one whose mind is pervaded by desire and the like does not perceive an object—even when it is in close proximity to the senses and situated in the midst of abundant light.

Regarding objects such as atoms, subtlety itself is the obstacle, because even one whose mind is directed toward them does not perceive them. In the perception of external objects such as walls, that very obstruction is the obstacle, just as the hand or other limbs are obstacles in the perception of an object already grasped.
In some cases there is *abhibhava* (overpowering), as when the eye is unable to perceive the stars, the sun, or other planets during the day because they are overwhelmed by the rays of the sun.

In some cases there is *samānābhihāra* (confusion with the similar), which is unfavorable, as when the eye lacks the capacity to perceive individual drops of water released from a cloud into a body of water.

In some cases there is *anudbhava* (non-manifestation), as when, in the state of milk turning into curd and so forth, one lacks the capacity to distinguish between the curd, the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and other components.

This being the case, when perception does not operate toward an object already established by other more firm means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one of these [other means] is postulated as the obstructing factor; it is not that there is a non-operation [of perception] simply due to the absence of that object.
And it has been said by the founder of the Sāṅkhya school: "Its non-perception is due to subtlety, not due to non-existence.
Now, while in some cases that which is established by perception becomes an object of inference because of doubt, this [subtle object] lacks such [doubt]; therefore, [you claim] its non-existence.
If it is argued that this is not so, we reply: it is accepted by all disputants that an effect indeed serves as the means for inferring its cause;

thus, since the existence of the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is established precisely through the impossibility of explaining effects such as the "Great One" (*mahat*) otherwise, its non-existence is not tenable.
Now, one might object: if a cause is established through the impossibility of explaining an effect otherwise, then the cause intended by other systems will also be established.

If it is argued that the *pradhāna* as conceived by you is not established, we say no; for upon examining the doctrine, only that view which is set forth in the *Kapila-sūtras* and is consistent with the proofs for *pradhāna* is tenable through reasoning. Any other [view], however, like the doctrines of the outsiders (*bāhya*), is merely a semblance of a doctrine (*matābhāsa*) and must be refuted.
For example: "The existent is born from the non-existent."

Thus, the establishment of *pradhāna* in the Buddhist view—based on the principle that "the existent arises from the existent"—is not sufficient to adorn the mouths of the learned, because it contradicts the Sāṅkhya doctrine; for the causal relationship between the existent and the non-existent is impossible. How could a non-existent, unreal cause produce effects consisting of sound and so forth, which are of the nature of existence? This is because identity (*tādātmya*) is observed between the existent and the non-existent.

For it is well-established in cases such as threads and cloth that an effect is inherent in its cause; and if this were so, every user of language would employ expressions such as "the jar is non-existent" or "the cloth is non-existent," meaning that everything would be perceived as inherent in non-existence. Consequently, there would be no cognition of the world as qualified by existence, such as "this is existent. Now, as for the Vedāntic view that this phenomenal world is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the Existent (*sat*): [this is the position to be addressed].
That too is incorrect; for by this [view] as well, the established doctrine that "the existent arises from the existent" would not be proven.

If the non-dual appears as having duality, it would be nothing but an illusion—just like the appearance of a rope as a garland, a fragment, or a snake—because its object is sublated, like the cognition of a snake in a rope. Since the knowledge of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would thus lack validity, knowledge in the form of valid cognition (*pramā*) itself would come to an end.

Nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), for through the perception of the teacher’s and disciple’s subsequent questions and answers as invalid, there would be the total destruction of mere worldly discourse; and since the engagement of anyone in the performance of worldly and Vedic activities would be impossible, there would be neither worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) nor liberation (*apavarga*), and thus that scripture would lose its authority.
Furthermore, it would constitute a deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*), for in the Vedānta view, Brahman does not undergo illusory transformation (*vivarta*). And it has been said:
"For the ignorant, this entire world is an evolution (vivarta) of Brahman;
the wise, however, always abide in the non-evolved bliss.

Thus, the view of Kaṇabhakṣa (Kaṇāda) and Akṣacaraṇa (Gautama), that "from the existent the non-existent is born"—meaning that from the existent atom (paramāṇu) the non-existent effect called the dyad (dvyaṇuka) is produced—is also [refuted].

This is not tenable; for since the atom is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), and the dyad is non-existent, then because there is no difference in their non-existence, the atom would also be the inherent cause of things such as a rabbit's horn. Thus, the existent and the non-existent would be identical.
And because it arises from effort,
it is unreal; [therefore] there is identity with that.
If it were heated,
would it be existent or non-existent?
The non-existence prior [to production] named "prior non-existence" (prāgabhāva).
It possesses threefold existence, but unlike wind, form, and so forth, it does not lack existence throughout the three times.
If it is argued that this is so,
[we ask]: what is this "prior"?
Is the non-existence of the counter-correlativity of an entity [prior to its production]? What [is it]? Prior...
Because it is the counter-correlate of existence, it is non-existence.
Alternatively, it is the state of being the counter-positive of prior non-existence with respect to reality.
Is it not the case that today [the existence] of all functional things and categories is non-existent?
Because there is no distinction in reality, [it is] just like space-flowers and the like,
by virtue of their very non-existence.
Even for them, there would be linguistic usage prior [to that].
Because it is the counter-correlate of an entity, and thus likewise.
The negation of effects, substances, qualities, universals, and so forth.
It might be that their existence is [established] by way of being a property of entities through non-existence.
Because of its location; and not because of the hair of a tortoise or similar things.
There may be a distinction [of the particular] from the universal and so forth.
There is no distinction by way of existence, because of the absence of any property; nor is there one by way of form.
Because of the non-existence [of the effect] prior [to its production], there is antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
If [non-existence] were a triadic relation, then even for things such as a human horn, there would be prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
There would be antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) of its being a triadic relation.

Furthermore, because of the rule that [an effect] must necessarily produce its own corresponding [cause], everything non-existent would become existent; thus, the distinction between the existent and the non-existent in the world would be as good as abandoned by pouring water over it. Therefore, the doctrine of the Tārkika-Vaiśeṣikas is not able to withstand scrutiny.
Therefore, the Sāṅkhya doctrine alone—that "from the existent, the existent is born"—is consistent with reason.

From an existent cause, the effect, which is already existent even prior to its own production, attains manifestation through the operation of the cause. Nor should it be argued that this results in proving what is already established or that the cause is rendered useless; for even though the effect exists, the cause is purposeful in bringing about its manifestation, and thus there is no fault whatsoever.

In the view that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryapakṣa*), however, the futility of the cause is quite evident; for it is impossible to establish a relationship between a cause and that which is non-existent.
Only that which is related can be produced by what is unrelated; if that which is unrelated were produced, everything would arise from everything, and the restriction of causes would vanish.

If an effect were non-existent, it could not come into existence through the operation of a cause. As stated in the *Tattvakaumudī*: "Indeed, even with a thousand crafts, it is impossible to make blue yellow.

Nor can it be argued that before the operation of the cause the jar was non-existent and after the operation it is existent, such that existence and non-existence are properties (*dharma*) of the jar; for since a property is a characteristic of an entity (*bhāvadharma*), the existence of the substratum (*dharmin*) follows from that very fact, as its own persistence would otherwise be untenable.
It has been established that the effect is indeed existent even prior to the operation of the cause, as if it were after such operation.

The operation of the cause, however, is not otherwise accounted for (i.e., is not redundant) in respect to its manifestation. Furthermore, in other cases as well, manifestation is seen to result from the operation of a cause, such as the manifestation of rice-grains through the threshing of paddy, of oil from sesame seeds through pressing, and [milk] through milking.
Regarding the phrase "the milk of cows":
there is no example for the arising of what was previously non-existent; therefore, the effect exists [prior to its production] and is merely manifested by the operation of the cause.
Because it is impossible for that which is non-existent to have a connection with a cause, the cause cannot be its producer. And so it has been stated by the Sāṅkhya teachers.
Because it is non-existent, there is no connection with causes that are associated with existence.
And for one who desires the arising of that which is unconnected, there is no established order.

Furthermore, even when connected, a cause produces only that for which it is capable; and this capacity is to be understood solely through the effect, just as visual cognition occurs only through the eye and not through another sense organ—it is precisely from this that it is understood that "this [organ] alone is capable" in that regard. Now, would such a capacity reside in the capable cause, reside in the capable effect, or reside everywhere?
In the latter case, everything would arise from everything.

Now, if that potency resides in the effect, then how can the non-existent effect be the locus of potency? Furthermore, that which is produced by a potent cause must itself be capable [of being produced], and the capable is of the nature of the cause; since the cause is existent, how could the effect—which is non-different from it—be non-existent? And it has been said:
"Because that which is capable produces only what is possible for it";

and because the relationship of material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) is perceived, there is no difference between the threads and the cloth. For those two things between which there is no difference, there is no relationship of material cause and effect, as in the case of a horse and a tree. For this reason also, the threads and the cloth are not distinct entities, because neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is observed; if they were distinct entities, conjunction would [necessarily] occur.

In the case of a rope, a jar, a bowl, or jujube fruits and the like, conjunction is observed; yet non-reachability (aprāpti) is also observed, as between Mount Sumeru and Mount Vindhya. Furthermore, since neither conjunction nor non-reachability exists here [between the threads and the cloth], the cloth is not an entity distinct from the threads. And the Sāṅkhya teachers have stated the proof establishing the non-difference between cause and effect, as follows: "The cloth is not [distinct] from the threads..."
It is distinct because it is its property; for whatever is distinct from something here does not become a property of that thing, just as a cow is not a property of a horse.

And since a cloth is a property of threads, it is therefore not a different entity [from them]. Furthermore, because no additional weight is perceived, the effect is not a different entity from the cause.

Thus, non-difference being established, it is the threads themselves that, having undergone transformation through various specific configurations (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*), constitute the cloth; the cloth is not a separate entity from the threads.
Nor should it be argued that the difference between cause and effect is established by the difference in self-referential cognition and the difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*);
for even in a single entity, such differences in self-referential cognition and causal efficiency are possible through the manifestation and disappearance of other particularities.
The establishment of difference [between cause and effect] follows from the impossibility of [the observed facts] being otherwise.
In that regard, even for a single tortoise, its limbs emerge and become manifest when they come forth, and those very same limbs disappear when they enter back into the body of the tortoise;
yet those limbs of the tortoise are neither produced nor destroyed. In the same way, even for a single piece of gold or clay, [there arise] bracelets, earrings, and so forth.

Objects such as jars, when emerging, undergo the conventional designation of "arising," and those very same objects, when entering [into their causal state], are said to "disappear" or "perish"; however, there is no demonstration of the cessation of the existent or the arising of the non-existent.
And it has been said by the Blessed One: "The existence of the non-existent is not found, nor is the non-existence of the existent found."
Just as a tortoise is not distinct from its own limbs which undergo contraction and expansion, so too bracelets, earrings, and the like are not distinct from clay, gold, and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that the difference between cause and effect is established by the differences in cognition and functional efficiency (*arthakriyā*), for this is contradicted by the case of an actor (*naṭa*).
For an actor, having himself assumed infinite names—such as "I am Daśaratha," "I am Rāma," or "I am Yudhiṣṭhira"—appears under various other names.
It assumes another dress and performs another purposeful action; and even though these three types of difference exist, because no difference in the actor is perceived, as they have said:
"The form, the action, and the designation of the actor are each known to be distinct."
Does the actor not attain distinctness [from his roles]?
This must necessarily be answered by those who are skilled.

Even for a single fire, a variety of causal functions is observed through the distinction between its capacity to burn and its capacity to cook; yet, by this much, the fire does not undergo differentiation. Just as each individual blade of grass lacks the power to prevent heat and rain, yet when many are combined and attain a particular state, those very same blades acquire the power to prevent them, so too is it with the one.

In this way, although the threads are capable of performing functions such as covering and so forth, it is they themselves, when combined and having reached a particular state, that—having manifested the nature of a cloth—will perform the function of covering and so on. Therefore, the effect exists even before [manifestation] from its cause; it is simply that there is a manifestation of it.
Now, is this manifestation existent or non-existent prior to the operation of the cause?

If you argue that in the first case (if the effect already exists) there is no possibility for the operation of causes—for no one employs causes for the production of what already exists—and in the second case (if it does not exist) the consequence follows that only the non-existent is produced, we reply: even for you, what is this "production"—is it existent or non-existent?
In the first case, we see no purpose for the causal operation.

In the final case, there is the arising of the non-existent; thus, since "it arises," there must be another arising for that arising, and yet another for that as well—clearly, this results in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Alternatively, if that arising is not distinct from the cloth, then when one says "cloth," one should not further say "it arises," because of redundancy.
Likewise, having said "it arises," one should not further say "cloth" for the very same reason of the aforementioned fault. [The cloth...]

Nor can it be said that [the cloth] perishes, because that would involve a contradiction. Therefore, the production of the cloth must be either its inherence in its own existence or its inherence in its own cause; yet, since inherence is eternal, the production of the cloth is impossible in either case. Furthermore, causes are not employed for the sake of such production.
Thus, since there is merely the manifestation of an already existent cloth and so forth, there is no fault whatsoever in the dependence upon causes.

Furthermore, the cause cannot be connected with the effect in the form of a cloth or the like, because that [effect] is inactive; for causal factors are connected with action, otherwise their status as "factors" (kārakas) would be undermined. Therefore, it is established that the effect pre-exists (satkārya). Since the means to overcome the threefold suffering is the knowledge of the difference between Nature (prakṛti) and the Spirit (puruṣa), the dissimilarity of the Manifest (vyakta) must be demonstrated for its utility.

And that Manifest—consisting of earth and the other elements—is distinct from the Unmanifest Pradhāna; since this [Manifest] possesses a cause, it is therefore non-eternal and becomes latent through the very same collection of conditions for destruction that others [the opponents] accept.
Furthermore, the cause pervades the effect, but the effect does not pervade the cause.

Moreover, the intellect and the other faculties are active; they abandon the body acquired in each preceding birth and take up another body. This very activity belongs to them, whereas the activity of earth and the other elements is well known in the form of transformation.

Due to the diversity of the intellect and so forth for each individual, this [activity] is manifold; likewise, due to the distinctions between jars, bodies, and so on, earth and the other elements are also manifold.

Although there is no relationship of locus and located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) between intellect (*buddhi*) and the other [evolutes] because there is no difference in their primary nature (*pradhāna*), nevertheless, by some means intended to express a distinction, a relationship of locus and located may be posited—just as one says, "The *tilaka* trees are here in this forest. However, there is no conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between the primary nature and the cognition of its parts and the whole, because they are identical in essence (*tādātmya*). Nor is there conjunction among the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, because conjunction is the attainment of what was previously unattained, and such a state does not exist here;
it is indeed eternal.
The dependent nature acts toward its own effect.
In that which is called the syllable *ṅka*, one should naturally fill the *ja* and *na*.
Otherwise, she would have perished before your eyes.
The syllable "na" is the letter *ṅ*.
*Ja* is *na*.
O you who are capable of protecting,
do not be afraid.
The syllable *thāḥ* also [is effective] in its own function.
The ritual action is fulfilled; it does not depend on anything else.
The mere cause itself is [the object].

When an effect is to be produced, it requires dependence upon that [cause]; likewise, the manifest (vyakta) is dependent on another when its own effect is to be produced. That which was stated up to the word "because" (yataḥ) is the opposite of that, namely the unmanifest (avyakta). Although the unmanifest possesses activity characterized by transformation (pariṇāma), it nevertheless lacks locomotion (parispanda).
Now, the similarity between the manifest and the unmanifest, and their dissimilarity from the Puruṣa, must be established.
The manifest is indeed "three-guṇa" (triguṇa), meaning it possesses the three guṇas whose nature consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Here, because there is no difference between cause and effect, the terms "pleasure" and so forth denote sattva and the other guṇas; by the statement "three-guṇa," it should be understood that the view held by opponents—that sattva and the others are qualities of the Self—is refuted.

Likewise, they are non-discriminative (*aviveki*); just as the *pradhāna* is not distinguished from existence (*sat*), so too the *mahat* and the others are not distinguished from the *pradhāna*, because they share its essential nature.
Alternatively, non-discrimination means acting in combination; for no single factor is capable of producing an effect by itself, but rather all together, each performing its entire function.
Thus, the *pradhāna*, the intellect (*buddhi*), and the rest are all insentient (*acetana*), and likewise possess the property of productivity (*prasava*).
It should be understood that these manifest attributes have been described as belonging to the unmanifest as well; this alone constitutes the similarity between the manifest and the unmanifest.

Thus, the Manifest and the Unmanifest have been defined through their similarities and differences; since the Puruṣa is devoid of the properties belonging to both of those, he is the "opposite" (viparīta). This constitutes the Puruṣa’s dissimilarity to the Manifest and the Unmanifest. Now, one might object: "Is it not perceived that the Puruṣa shares a similarity with Pradhāna in such qualities as being causeless (ahetumat) and eternal (anitya)? Likewise, his multiplicity (anekatva) is indeed a similarity with the Manifest. This being the case, how can the Puruṣa be said to be the opposite of the Manifest and the Unmanifest? If this is asked, the answer is: No, because [the claim of] similarity regarding causelessness and so forth...
Even so, there is no fault, because it indeed possesses a dissimilarity [from the intellect] due to its lack of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*).
Nor is the "three qualities" unestablished; for the teachers of Sāṃkhya maintain that the qualities (*guṇa*) consist of pleasure, pain, and dejection.

Here, in sequence: pleasure is happiness, and that itself is *sattva*; likewise, pain is displeasure, and the quality of *rajas* consists of displeasure; similarly, dejection is delusion, and the quality of *tamas* consists of dejection.

In the view that pleasure (*prīti*) is the absence of pain (*duḥkhābhāva*), and likewise that pain is the absence of pleasure, the author of the root text has included the term "self" (*ātman*) for the purpose of excluding those [absences]. Since the word "self" denotes a positive entity (*bhāvatattva*), there is no circular dependence; otherwise, not even one of them would be established. Furthermore, it should be understood that their respective purposes are, in order: illumination (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and restraint (*niyamana*).

If the lightness of *sattva* were led everywhere by the active *rajas*, like a tuft of cotton by a violent wind, it would never cease; however, because there is restraint by the heavy *tamas*, [the mind] is restricted. Being restrained by *tamas*, it functions only in certain instances;
therefore, *tamas* exists for the purpose of restriction. Thus, they have the nature of mutually overcoming one another.

Among these, by the power of the object, one or another becomes predominant and overcomes the others; for example, when *sattva* overcomes *rajas* and *tamas*, it attains its own peaceful state of activity (*vṛtti*). Likewise, when *rajas* overcomes *sattva* and *tamas*, it enters a terrible state of activity;
and similarly, when *tamas* overcomes *sattva* and *rajas*, it enters a deluded state.
Likewise, they function through mutual dependence, as it has been said:

"Sattva, depending upon activity (pravṛtti) and restraint (niyama), assists rajas and tamas by means of illumination (prakāśa); rajas, depending upon illumination and restraint, assists the other two by means of activity; and tamas, depending upon illumination and activity, assists the other two by means of restraint."
Likewise, they function through mutual production;
one produces another, and here "production" consists in their quantitative measure, which is of a similar form among the qualities (*guṇas*).
For this very reason, there is no state of having a cause, because there is no cause that is a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*).
Nor is there impermanence [in them], because there is no dissolution into another reality (tattvāntara), and because their mutual designations are subject to deviation. And it has been said:
"All are mutual companions; all go everywhere."
Sattva is the mate of rajas; rajas is the mate of sattva.
And within that pair of *tamas*, both *sattva* and *rajas* also exist;
their state of being a pair consists in their association and their non-deviation from one another.
"The union of the two—sattva and rajas—is called tamas;
no beginning, conjunction, or disjunction of these is perceived.
However, their specific functions are as follows: lightness and illumination belong to sattva alone, and not to either of the other two.

In this context, the quality that serves as the cause for upward movement is lightness (*lāghava*), which is incompatible with heaviness (*gaurava*); it is because of this that fire moves with its flames directed upwards.
That same quality is the cause for the horizontal movement of certain things, such as the wind.

Similarly, lightness is the cause for the proficiency of the organs in their functions; for if they were heavy, they would be sluggish. Thus, the nature of *sattva* has been described as being characterized by luminosity.
Sattva and tamas, languishing due to their lack of activity in producing their own effects, are supported by rajas;
being freed from this languor, they are made to exert effort toward enthusiasm. And it has been said:
"Sattva is held to be light and illuminating, while rajas is stimulating and mobile."

From what [cause] is there support, such that [the guṇa] is mobile? If rajas, by its mobility, were to set the entire triad of qualities (traiguṇya) in motion everywhere, there would be no obstruction therein by the heavy, concealing tamas; however, because it is turned away from this and that by tamas, it is set in motion only in a specific direction—thus, tamas is the regulator.
As they have said: "Heaviness and obscuration is indeed *tamas*";
likewise, lightness and illumination is *sattva* alone, while support and mobility is *rajas* alone, and heaviness and obscuration is *tamas* alone.

If it is objected that since the *guṇas* are by nature mutually antagonistic, it is only logical that they should cancel one another out according to the maxim of Sundopasunda, and not perform a single common function—[we reply: no, for even such [mutually opposed] things can indeed perform a single common function.
Because of this demonstration: for example, just as a wick and oil, which are opposed to fire, yet when combined with fire, perform the function characterized by the illumination of form;
and just as wind, bile, and phlegm, though by nature mutually antagonistic, when combined, perform the function of sustaining the body.
Likewise, although sattva, rajas, and tamas possess contradictory natures, they will coexist together and, having combined, will perform a single function by virtue of the purpose of the Puruṣa.
And it has been said: "Their functioning is for the sake of the object, like a lamp."
Because the qualities (*guṇa*) have the primary nature (*pradhāna*) as their essence, there is diversity even within unity, appearing in the form of the suppressed and the suppressor.

It has been said: "A single woman, endowed with virtue, lineage, beauty, character, and youth, brings happiness to her husband; for what reason? Because the form of happiness arises toward him from her. Yet she causes suffering to her co-wives; for what reason? Toward them..."
Because the form of suffering arises toward her in that very way, she thus deludes another man who does not find her;
for what reason? Because the form of delusion arises toward him from her.
By means of this woman, all phenomena (bhāvas) are explained.

In this regard, that which is the cause of pleasure is *sattva* itself, whose nature is pleasure; likewise, that which is the cause of pain is *rajas*, whose nature is pain; and that which is the cause of delusion is *tamas*, whose nature is delusion.
Therefore, the effect exists even prior to the operation of its causes;
it merely becomes manifest through their activity, just as the limbs of a tortoise, though already existing, emerge and become distinct.
This is the body of the tortoise, these are its limbs; by him they were contracted and thus became unmanifest within it.

Likewise, from clay, gold, and so forth, jars, earrings, and the like—which already exist—become manifest and are differentiated, such that one says, "this is clay" and "this is its effect, the jar," and so on.

Likewise, the elements such as earth and the rest, already existing, manifest from their cause, the *tanmātras*, and are differentiated [such that] "this is the cause of this" and "this is the effect of this. Similarly, the *tanmātras*, already existing, manifest from the *ahaṅkāra* and are differentiated. In this way, the *ahaṅkāra*, already existing, becomes manifest from the *mahat*, and the *mahat*, already existing, proceeds to manifestation from the *mūlaprakṛti*.

Thus is the differentiation of the manifested universe (*prapañca*), which is the effect, from the supreme unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is the cause—whether directly or through a succession. Just as a jar, a bowl, or other objects, upon entering a lump of clay or a lump of gold, become unmanifest; though they were manifest in the form of their cause, they cease to be manifest in the form of their effects; so too do earth and the other elements, upon entering the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), [cease to be manifest] in their own specific forms.

The subtle elements (tanmātras) manifest their own cause by means of their own nature; yet, although that cause is manifested, it does not manifest its own form as an effect within itself. In this way, the subtle elements enter into the ego (ahaṅkāra) and manifest the ego according to their own perspective. Likewise, the ego, entering into the Great Principle (mahat), manifests the Great Principle; and the Great Principle [manifests] its own cause, the Pradhāna.
Entering it, the unmanifest manifests that [effect]; however, there is no entry of the Pradhāna anywhere because it is not an effect, but rather it is the unmanifest cause of all effects.
Thus is the non-differentiation.
Such are the differentiation and non-differentiation of the universe within Prakṛti.

Some, having taken the unmanifest (avyakta), or the great principle (mahat), or the ego (ahaṅkāra), or the senses, or the elements as the Self, worship those very things; however, they are to be refuted in the manner that will be explained.

There exists a Person (puruṣa) distinct from the unmanifest and the rest, because the unmanifest, the great principle, the ego, and so forth exist for the sake of another. Why? Because of their being composite entities (saṅghātatva). Whatever is a composite entity is seen to be for the sake of another, like oil, betel, ghee, curds, milk, food, clothing, and so on.
All composite entities (saṅghāta) consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion; therefore, that for whose sake these composites exist is the Puruṣa.
Now, as for the objection: "It is observed that composites such as beds and seats serve the purpose of another body which is itself a composite, but they do not serve their own selves;
therefore, [the reason] would only establish another composite and not the non-composite Self"—this is not correct, because of the nature of the composite.

If it were for the sake of another aggregate, then because that [second] one is also an aggregate, it too would have to be for the sake of another aggregate; and because that one is also an aggregate, it would likewise require another, leading to an insurmountable infinite regress.
Furthermore, there is an invariable concomitance (vyāpti) between being an aggregate and being for the sake of another in general, but not specifically with being for the sake of another aggregate.
Nor should it be said that [a property] is to be inferred in such a way simply because it has been observed in an example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

For if one were to accept an inference that establishes every property observed in the example within the subject of the thesis (*dārṣṭāntika*), then all inference would be destroyed; this is because properties such as "being a kitchen" found in the kitchen-example and so forth do not exist on the mountain and other such subjects.

As they have said: "Properties such as 'consisting of the three qualities' (*triguṇatva*) are pervaded by 'being a composite'; these, when excluded from this [subject], namely the Supreme (*para*), exclude 'consisting of the three qualities' and so forth, just as the exclusion of 'Brahminhood' excludes [sub-classes] such as 'being a Kaṭha'."

The existence of the *puruṣa* is established also by way of superintendence (*adhiṣṭhāna*), because the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, which consist of the three *guṇas*, are superintended [by something else].
Just as a chariot and such are superintended by means of a driver and so forth, so too the intellect and the rest—which consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion—must be superintended by another.

Furthermore, the existence of the *puruṣa* is to be understood from the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛbhāva*); for pleasure and pain, which are objects of enjoyment, are experienced by each individual as agreeable and disagreeable sensations; therefore, by virtue of their being agreeable and disagreeable...
Or there must be some experiencer;

nor should it be said that cognition and so forth themselves are such [an experiencer], for since they consist of pleasure and the like, if they were to know themselves by themselves, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya).

The existence of the Puruṣa is established even by the fact that activity toward the goal of isolation (*kaivalya*) occurs. Isolation, characterized by the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering, cannot belong to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties; for they consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion—how could they be separated from their own nature? Therefore, because the scriptures and the great-minded engage in activity for the sake of isolation, there exists [the Puruṣa] distinct from the intellect and the rest.
By the term "self," the existence of the person (*puruṣa*) is established.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the self is thus established as distinct from cognition and the other faculties, is it nevertheless different for each body or is it one and the same? We reply: it is indeed different, because multiplicity alone is possible, since otherwise the regularity of birth, death, and so forth could not be accounted for.

And it has been stated by the Sāṃkhya teachers: "The plurality of Puruṣas is established from the specific determination of birth, death, and the instruments (of perception and action), from their non-simultaneous activity, and indeed from the variation in the three guṇas."
Birth is the Puruṣa’s connection with a new set of body, senses, mind, ego, intellect, and sensations, distinguished by their specific genus;

it is not a transformation of the Puruṣa, because he is unchanging. Death is the relinquishing of those very same acquired things—the body and so forth—not the destruction of the Self, because that eternally immutable Self is permanent.

The thirteen instruments, beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*), have a fixed order or arrangement regarding their birth, death, and functioning; however, this [arrangement] is not possible if there were only one Puruṣa in all bodies. For if that were the case, when one person is happy, all would be happy, or when one is suffering, all would suffer; likewise, when one dies, all would die, and when one is born, all would be born.

And if [cognition] were produced [independently], then in the case of one person who is blind or deaf, everyone would likewise be so; but this is not the case. Similarly, if there were no distinction between persons, then when one is distracted (*vicitta*), all would be distracted, resulting in a lack of systematic order (*avyavasthā*). However, when there is a distinction between persons (*puruṣabheda*), such systematic order is properly established. Nor should it be argued that even for a single person, systematic order is indeed possible by virtue of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of different bodies; for if that were so, there would also be a systematic order regarding birth, death, and so forth, based on the differences between hands, feet, breasts, and other parts [of the same body].
The plurality of the *puruṣas* is also to be understood from the inversion of the three *guṇas*.
For example: some abound in *sattva*, such as those who flow upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*); some abound in *rajas*, such as human beings; and some abound in *tamas*, such as those born as animals.

Just as there is a plurality of *puruṣas*, so too their lack of the three *guṇas*, their discriminative nature, their non-objectivity, their uniqueness, their sentience, their lack of productivity, and their state of being witnesses and so forth are to be understood.

This creation is produced by the conjunction of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*; and that conjunction is not possible between two distinct entities without mutual dependence. Furthermore, the dependence of *pradhāna* on the *puruṣa* is for the sake of its own manifestation; for *pradhāna* is an object of experience by virtue of its nature as an objective field (*viṣaya*), and experience does not occur without an experiencer. Thus, there is a dependence of *pradhāna* upon the *puruṣa*. On the other hand, the dependence of the *puruṣa* is for the sake of its own liberation (*kaivalya*).

The Puruṣa depends upon Pradhāna; for the Puruṣa, being conjoined with the object of experience (bhogya) that is Pradhāna, imagines the threefold suffering residing therein as belonging to its own self and thus seeks isolation (kaivalya). That isolation, however, has as its cause the discriminative discernment of the difference between Sattva and Puruṣa, and such discernment of the difference between Sattva and Puruṣa does not occur without Pradhāna. Thus, the conjunction of both occurs through the Puruṣa’s dependence on Pradhāna, like the union of the lame man and the blind man.

Even though [the self] was previously joined with a succession of enjoyments and so forth, it is again joined for the sake of isolation (kaivalya). And that conjunction, without the creation of the Great One (mahat) and the rest, is not capable of bringing about either enjoyment or liberation; therefore, conjunction itself brings about the creation of the Great One and the rest. And it has been said: "From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One; from that, the I-maker (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen."
From those five among the sixteen [elements], the five gross elements arise.
The group consisting of the eleven organs and the five subtle elements (tanmātras), numbering sixteen, is called the "sixteenfold" (ṣoḍaśaka).

And it has been stated therein that from the subtle element of sound arises ether, which has sound as its quality; and from the subtle element of touch, accompanied by the subtle element of sound, arises air, which possesses the qualities of both sound and touch.
From the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra) accompanied by the subtle elements of sound and touch, fire arises, possessing the qualities of sound, touch, and form;
from the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra) accompanied by the subtle elements of sound, touch, and form, water arises, possessing the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste;

and from the subtle element of smell (gandha-tanmātra) accompanied by the subtle elements of sound, touch, form, and taste, earth arises, possessing the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

Intellection (*buddhi*) is determination (*adhyavasāya*). The designation [of the intellect] as both the action and the agent is due to the intention to express their non-difference. Virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*virāga*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) are the *sāttvika* qualities of the intellect; their opposites, such as non-virtue (*adharma*) and so forth, are *tāmasa*.
From the quality of sovereignty, which is a property of the intellect, there arises the manifestation of the powers (*siddhis*) such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest. And that...

"Atomicity (aṇimā), magnificence (mahimā), heaviness (garimā), lightness (laghimā), as well as reach (prāpti), irresistible will (prākāmya), lordship (īśitva), and mastery (vaśitva)—these are the eight perfections (siddhis). Now, it may be asked: does not the creation proceeding from the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) consist of two kinds—the group of eleven organs and the five subtle elements (tanmātras)?

Furthermore, as for what was said—that how can there be a creation of such a diverse nature, consisting of both luminous and insentient elements, from a single cause that is the *ahaṅkāra*—that is not correct. From the *sāttvika* *ahaṅkāra*, the group of eleven organs arises due to its luminosity and lightness;
however, from the *tāmasa* *ahaṅkāra*, known as *bhūtādi*, the group of subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arises.
Although the ego (ahaṅkāra) is one, it nevertheless performs distinct functions due to the emergence and suppression of the [guṇas].

Now, if creation is produced by *sattva* and *tamas* alone, then what is the use of *rajas*, which would be rendered ineffective? No; for the author of the root-text states, "From the *taijasa* both arise.
From the *taijasa* (the rājasa ego) both groups of principles arise—that is, the two types of creation belonging to *sattva* and *tamas*.

Although there is no other specific effect of *rajas*, nevertheless, although *sattva* and *tamas* are themselves inactive and capable [in themselves], they do not produce an effect; however, when set in motion by *rajas*, they become capable of producing their own effects through its assistance— thus both are dependent on *rajas*.
As they have said: "In both types of effects, since passion (rajas) functions as a cause by means of generating activity within both goodness (sattva) and darkness (tamas), it is not useless.
— Examination of the Senses.
Praise to the one who has composed the *Tattvapradīpa*.
Thus, for fear of prolixity,
it is not elaborated here.
They are: Ma, Ha, Da, Ha,
Ṅkāra, Ma.
Its internal faculties do not exist; they are their own specific characteristics.
Those whose characteristics are common are called "having their own characteristics" (svalakṣaṇa).
And that great realization must be deeply contemplated.
The conceit of "I" (ahaṃkāra) is self-importance.

*Saṅkalpa* is a modification (*vṛtti*), that is, an activity (*vyāpāra*) of the mind. He states that these [modifications] are of two kinds—common and uncommon—with the words: "This very [modification] is uncommon. This aforementioned [modification] is the uncommon one; however, the common modification of the instruments (*karaṇa*) consists of the five vital airs (*prāṇa* etc.). These five airs are the modification of the three instruments; they constitute life (*jīvana*), because when they exist, [the body] exists, and when they are absent, [it] is absent.
And because of their non-existence [elsewhere], there are five vital airs (*vāyu*):

among them, *prāṇa* functions in the tip of the nose, the heart, the navel, and the big toes; *apāna* functions in the nape of the neck, the back, the sides, the anus, and the genitals; *samāna* functions in the heart, the navel, and all the joints; *udāna* functions in the heart, the throat, the root of the palate, the head, and the middle of the eyebrows; and *vyāna* functions in the skin. Thus are the five vital airs.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is fivefold; thus, ignorance, egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and clinging to existence (*abhiniveśa*) are respectively designated as darkness (*tamas*), delusion (*moha*), great delusion (*mahāmoha*), gloom (*tāmisra*), and utter gloom (*andhatāmisra*). This constitutes the five-fold [ignorance]. Although the creation of the intellect (*pratyayasarga*) and its subdivisions exist, they are not demonstrated here for fear of excessive prolixity. "The creation of the intellect" means the creation of *buddhi*. And it has been said: "This creation of the intellect is known by the names error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment. It is called *pratyaya* because one perceives (*pratīyate*) by means of it; that which is the creation of that *pratyaya*, the intellect, is the "creation of the intellect" (*pratyayasarga*).
The divine creation (*daivasarga*), however, has been clearly explained by the author himself.
That eightfold divine creation consists of the following eight varieties: the Brāhma, Prājāpatya, Aindra, Paitrya, Gāndharva, Yākṣa, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca.
Furthermore, the animal births (*tiryagyonayaḥ*) are of five kinds: domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and immobile beings.
And the human [category] is of one kind, because—disregarding internal distinctions of caste such as Brahminhood and so forth—there is no difference in physical form among all four [castes].

Now, one might object: this creation belongs to the Pradhāna, and since the Pradhāna is insentient, how can it initiate activity for its own sake or for the sake of another? Therefore, there must be some sentient being who presides over Prakṛti.
Nor can the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) be such [presiders], because they are ignorant of the true nature of Prakṛti. Consequently, there exists a presider of Prakṛti.
If it is argued that "He who is omniscient is indeed Īśvara," we reply: even that which is insentient is seen to act for the sake of a purpose;
just as milk, though insentient, flows forth for the sake of the growth of the calf, so too will *prakṛti*, though inert, act for the sake of the liberation of the *puruṣa*.
Furthermore, regarding the activity of Īśvara, who is not an enjoyer, we see no motive other than compassion.

Furthermore, that desire to eliminate the suffering of others without regard for oneself—since there were no sentient beings prior to creation, there would be no suffering associated with them; for whose cessation, then, would the Lord’s activity be directed?
Nor can the Lord’s activity occur after creation, because since creation has already come into being, we see no purpose for the Lord.
Moreover, the cessation of suffering cannot be the purpose, for if his activity were for that sake, there would be no one at all in the world who suffers.

And it has been said: since the activity of a discerning person is pervaded by either self-interest or compassion, and since these two are absent in the case of the creation of the world, they necessarily exclude the quality of being preceded by the activity of a discerning person. For the Blessed One, who possesses all that is desired, would have no personal aim in creating the world; nor does his engagement in creation proceed from compassion, because prior to creation, the sense organs, bodies, and objects of experience for living beings have not yet arisen.

If there is an absence of suffering, for whom would there be a desire to abandon it? Compassion leads to creation, and creation results in compassion; thus, there is a circular dependency (*parasparāśraya*).
Furthermore, one who acts out of compassion would create only happy beings, not the destitute.

Nor can the diversity of the world be attributed to the diversity of karma, for if that were so, the diversity of the world would be established by that very [karma] alone, rendering God unnecessary. As for his activity, it is observed even in insentient things when driven by the purpose of serving another.
It is like milk [flowing] for the sake of the growth of the calf.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the purpose of the Person (puruṣārtha) is the motivator of Primordial Matter (prakṛti), we do not see anything that causes its cessation. If this is said, we reply: no; just as a dancer, having displayed her dance to the audience, ceases of her own accord, but not because of [an external agent].

Just as [a fire] requires another extinguisher for its own cessation, so too does Prakṛti— having manifested her own nature, consisting of sound and the rest, as distinct from the Puruṣa, and having thereby accomplished the purpose of the Puruṣa, cease of her own accord. As the Sāṃkhya teachers have said:
Just as a dancer ceases from her dance after displaying herself to the audience,
so does primordial nature (prakṛti) cease after manifesting herself to the Spirit (puruṣa).

[Objection: "But surely, just as a dancer who has performed her dance resumes it again out of a desire to please the spectators, so too Prakṛti, even after ceasing once she has shown herself to Puruṣa, might resume activity; if that were so, then even those who are liberated would undergo rebirth. [Reply:
No, for example, a virtuous wife who cannot endure the sight of another man—even if she is secluded from the sun's gaze—might, through negligence, have her garment fall from her body.

If she is observed by another man, then she behaves in such a way that she remains vigilant so that other men do not see her again; for even though a woman of good family is seen to be more than just her physical form (*prakṛti*), once she has been seen by a lover (*biṃbaka*), she does not come again within the range of sight. And it is said:
"It is my conviction that nothing exists more subtle than primordial nature (prakṛti),
which, once seen by the Spirit (puruṣa) thinking 'I have been seen,' does not present itself for sight again."
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—these are the sattvic qualities of the intellect (buddhi).
The four termed adharma, ignorance, passion, and lack of sovereignty are tāmasa.

Here, by means of these seven [qualities] excluding knowledge, prakṛti binds the self; yet by means of discriminative discernment—the knowledge of the distinctness between prakṛti and puruṣa—that very same [prakṛti] liberates it. And it has been said:
In this way, Nature binds herself to herself by means of the seven forms; and she alone, for the sake of the purpose of the Puruṣa, releases herself by means of a single form.

Just as the Most Compassionate Lord, assuming a playful form (*līlāvigraha*), set aside coral, gems, pearls, oyster shells, sea-monsters, tortoises, serpents, conchs, cowrie shells, and the like, and extracted only the jewels from the ocean for the sake of the prosperity of the gods; so too,

setting aside the fallacious arguments of sophistry (*jalpa-tarka-ābhāsa*) and the cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) which deals with objects of knowledge easily found elsewhere, [the Lord extracted] the jewels of the objects of knowledge obtainable solely through the *Sāṃkhya* system.

For those who are weary from the labor of studying the Sāṃkhya system, I have extracted these stories of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa from the ocean of the Sāṃkhya-tantra; may this lamp of the principles of Sāṃkhya remain upon the earth for as long as the moon and the sun endure.
Thus ends the *Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpa*, as elucidated by the ascetic Kavirāja, disciple of the venerable Vaikuṇṭha and disciple of the holy Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya.
